video_title: Grid cybersecurity: how big is the threat & what should we do about it?
gist: Patrick Miller, who co-wrote and first enforced the NERK CIP standards for the US bulk power grid, argues that Chinese state actors (Vault Typhoon) are demonstrably embedded and prepositioned inside US utilities but that a nationwide kill-switch blackout is astronomically improbable, while squirrels and mylar balloons remain orders of magnitude more damaging than cyber. The regulatory center of gravity is shifting to distribution: NERK just cut the generator registration threshold from 75 MVA at 100 kV to 20 MVA at 60 kV to capture inverter-based resources, VPPs and DER aggregators, and data centers dropping gigawatts at once (3 GW in PJM, 10 minutes to stabilize) are the newest all-hazards grid risk.

insights.claim: There is no documented US case of a cyber attacker directly causing grid damage; the confirmed intrusions are prepositioning, where attackers break in, hold access and wait.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: The bear case for grid-security spending rests on latent access, not realized loss, so budgets and regulation will stay reactive until a first damaging US incident occurs.
insights.quote: Most of these have been situations where the attacker is broken into the system and hasn't done any damage yet. They just preposition themselves.

insights.claim: Russia has caused actual blackouts on the Ukrainian grid more than once and recently in Poland, and Polish contacts say they have a long backlog of unpublished incidents, meaning public incident counts understate real attack frequency.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: European grid and utility security demand is driven by live, proven attacks rather than hypotheticals, and disclosed incident data materially undercounts the true rate.
insights.quote: when I talked to my contacts in Poland, they say they've got a a long list of things they just haven't published yet

insights.claim: Physical and natural threats to the grid, including squirrels, raccoons, snakes, scorpions, mylar balloons and rifle fire at transformers, cause far more damage than cyber attacks by orders of magnitude.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Risk-adjusted grid hardening dollars are better spent on ballistic protection and physical resilience than on the cyber narrative that dominates headlines.
insights.quote: Myar balloons, believe it or not, are actually a bigger threat than cyber.

insights.claim: North America has four separate grids joined by AC/DC ties and an incomprehensibly large diversity of field devices, making a nationwide or continent-scale hack-induced blackout astronomically improbable even with AI assistance, while targeted regional outages remain a real concern.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Investors should discount apocalyptic kill-switch scenarios in grid risk models and price regional, localized disruption instead.
insights.quote: Their ability to hack that diversity of systems is just it's impossible. Well, it's it's astronomically improbable.

insights.claim: Distributing generation across many diffuse assets actually reduces the physical threat because attackers cannot physically reach everywhere, so any single attack has smaller consequences.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: The common assumption that distributed energy strictly worsens grid risk is wrong on the physical axis, which supports the resilience case for DER deployment.
insights.quote: if you distribute the attack service to a much you know more diffuse uh set of assets you you actually take the threat away in a lot of cases because they physically can't get everywhere

themes.theme: OT devices and the patching bottleneck

insights.claim: Grid operational-technology devices are purpose-built firmware-and-configuration units with no operating system that were never designed to be networked, which makes them easier to hack than conventional IT systems rather than simpler to protect.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: OT security is an architecture and isolation problem, not a software-patching problem, which favors vendors selling network segmentation and monitoring over endpoint security tools.
insights.quote: you end up with devices that were never really meant to be connected that have some kind of connection to them

insights.claim: Updating grid OT devices requires rebooting them in almost all cases, and rebooting a device the grid depends on causes a blackout, so utilities must wait for maintenance windows and instead rely on extreme network isolation as the primary defense.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Known vulnerabilities in grid OT stay unpatched far longer than in IT, so mean-time-to-remediate assumptions imported from enterprise security are wrong for utility assets.
insights.quote: If this thing is required for the grid to run you don't just reboot it because you get a blackout.

insights.claim: AI is accelerating both sides of the vulnerability arms race, with attackers using it to find vulnerabilities in key grid equipment and manufacturers now using it to write patches for those same vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Vulnerability discovery rates in grid equipment should rise sharply, increasing demand for vendor patch pipelines and for utilities that can absorb faster update cadences.
insights.quote: AI is really good at finding vulnerabilities.

insights.claim: The industry has not yet solved how to operationalize faster patching of grid equipment and is considering scheduled public blackout windows or shifting power to redundant lines while systems restart, a practice utilities have never done before.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Watch for new operating practices and redundancy capex tied to patch windows; this is an unbudgeted operational change coming to utility planning.
insights.quote: we're in the process of that as an industry

themes.theme: NERK CIP scope and enforcement economics

insights.claim: The mandatory NERK CIP critical infrastructure protection standards cover no distribution assets at all and only some generation and transmission, contrary to the widespread belief that the whole US power grid is federally regulated for cyber security.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: The fastest-growing parts of the grid sit entirely outside the only mandatory, enforceable US grid cyber regime, which is the core regulatory gap to watch.
insights.quote: There is no distribution in scope at all.

insights.claim: The historical generation registration trigger was 75 MVA aggregate behind a single point of interconnection, and developers routinely sized facilities at 74.5 MVA specifically to stay under the compliance threshold.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Threshold-gaming is a predictable developer response, so any new threshold should be expected to bunch project sizes just below the line.
insights.quote: a lot of times they would even generate facilities to be 74.5 so they could get right under the threshold

insights.claim: Under CIP a system is classified as critical if its compromise or failure would impact the bulk power system within 15 minutes, which is the bright-line test determining a utility's entire compliance burden.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: The 15-minute impact test is the lever that decides which assets carry costly controls, so changes to it would swing utility compliance spend materially.
insights.quote: if it would cause an impact to that system within 15 minutes, that's a critical system

insights.claim: The CIP obligation stack spans security policies, personnel background screening and training, access revocation, an electronic firewall perimeter, physical lockdown, per-system hardening and logging, incident response and backup testing, configuration change control, information protection, supply chain vetting, encrypted control-center-to-control-center communications and, most recently adopted, monitoring of traffic between critical systems.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: The newly adopted internal network traffic monitoring requirement creates a fresh mandatory procurement category for OT network visibility vendors.

insights.claim: The CIP penalty ceiling has risen with inflation from one million to over 1.8 million dollars per day per violation but has never actually been levied, because settlements typically redirect penalty dollars into security improvements instead.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Headline fine exposure overstates realistic downside for utilities; the practical outcome is remediation capex, not cash penalties.
insights.quote: The number that gets thrown around is a million dollars per day per violation. That's actually gone up with inflation. It's over 1.8 million per day per violation. That's never been seen, though.

insights.claim: Enforcement authority flows from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission down to NERK as the electric reliability organization and out to six regional entities that audit utilities and send penalties back up the chain, and most in-scope systems land in the low-impact category with a reduced requirement set.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Compliance cost is concentrated in the minority of medium and high impact systems, so headline counts of registered entities overstate the real spending base.

themes.theme: Distribution, VPPs and the 20 MVA threshold

insights.claim: NERK has cut the generator registration threshold from 75 MVA connected at 100 kV transmission down to 20 MVA connected at 60 kV distribution, pulling distribution-connected inverter-based resources into federal registration for the first time.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: A large new cohort of commercial-scale solar and storage owners becomes federally registered, creating compliance-service demand and a new project-sizing constraint.
insights.quote: They took that down and now it's 20 MVA connected to a 60 KB system which is distribution.

insights.claim: Newly registered inverter-based resources must register and meet some obligations but face no security requirements yet, which Miller expects to change in the future.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Registration is the beachhead; security mandates on distributed generation are the next regulatory shoe to drop for DER developers and aggregators.
insights.quote: They don't have to do security things yet, but that's likely going to be coming in the future.

insights.claim: Federal jurisdiction over distribution-connected resources was hotly contested but upheld because regulators proved with physics, not speculation, that aggregated small resources can influence the interstate transmission system.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: The physics-proof precedent erodes the state-federal boundary and opens the door to further federal reach over distributed assets and multi-state VPPs.
insights.quote: they've actually done a pretty good job of proving it with physics. It's not just a speculation.

insights.claim: The inverter-based resource disturbances and blackouts in Texas and strain in California were grid physics problems rather than attacks, but regulators converged the physics finding with the security question of what happens if someone triggers the same behavior deliberately.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Reliability events, not cyber incidents, are what actually drive new grid security rules, so watch disturbance reports as the leading indicator of regulation.
insights.quote: These are just like, uh, grid physics problems.

insights.claim: Miller's team wrote lightweight cyber security baselines for distribution utilities and DER aggregators, based on the DHS cyber performance goals, requiring basics like no default credentials, no direct internet connection without a firewall, and multi-factor one-time codes for remote access, explicitly designed as a template states can copy into their own regulation.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: These voluntary baselines are the likely template for future state DER security rules, so aggregator platforms that already meet them face lower future compliance cost.
insights.quote: A blank page is always the hardest place to start.

insights.claim: The distribution and DER aggregator baselines are currently only a suggestion with no enforcement, functioning as a voluntary federal floor that states may or may not build on.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: There is no near-term mandatory compliance revenue in distribution cyber; adoption depends state by state, which fragments the addressable market.
insights.quote: At this point it's just a suggestion. It's a nice to have.

insights.claim: The 20 MVA threshold sweeps in warehouse-scale rooftop solar and battery owners who will never hire cyber security staff and whom regulators lack the capacity to audit, which forces the security burden down into the devices themselves at the supply chain level.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Secure-by-default device design becomes the only scalable answer, favoring inverter and battery vendors that can certify device-level security as a differentiator.
insights.quote: there's not enough to do the audits

insights.claim: The undocumented radios, modems and SIM card slots found inside Chinese solar inverters and batteries are in about 99 percent of cases artifacts of generic commodity motherboards bought by the million, not deliberately planted implants.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: The most-cited evidence for a Chinese inverter kill switch is largely explainable as commodity manufacturing, which argues against panic-driven rip-and-replace mandates.
insights.quote: Yes, it came with a radio. It came with a modem. It came with a place for a SIM card, there wasn't a SIM card inserted

insights.claim: Dormant hardware components on commodity boards could be activated remotely but would also need configuration and provisioning to function, similar to a phone needing an activated SIM, which raises the bar well above simply flipping a switch on a rogue device network.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: The practical difficulty of mass remote activation lowers the probability of a coordinated fleet-wide inverter attack relative to the popular narrative.
insights.quote: just because you turn something on doesn't mean it's ready to be used

insights.claim: The genuine supply chain risk sits at the software and firmware layer, where devices have been found phoning home and routing traffic through China, and that layer is where controls actually work because code can be inspected and updates gated before installation.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Policy and procurement leverage lands on software transparency and update control, creating demand for code inspection, SBOM and firmware attestation capabilities.
insights.quote: we're not just going to let updates from China happen without someone taking a look at it before it goes in

insights.claim: A wholesale ban on Chinese grid equipment, as discussed by the Trump administration, is a bad idea because Chinese gear is now genuinely high quality and performs to engineering spec, so ripping and replacing millions of installed units makes no sense.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Expect transparency and inspection regimes rather than blanket bans, which is far less disruptive to installed-base owners and to Chinese inverter suppliers than headlines imply.
insights.quote: It doesn't make sense to go rip and replace all this gear. They actually make quality stuff.

insights.claim: Miller's preferred approach is to live on a diet of poison fruit by accepting the imported hardware and either stripping out Chinese software and firmware to replace it with domestic code, or mandating transparency so batches can be sampled and certified as untainted.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: A firmware-replacement and batch-certification market could emerge as the pragmatic middle path between doing nothing and banning Chinese hardware.
insights.quote: is there a way to basically live on a diet of poison fruit

insights.claim: States including Texas and Florida have already banned certain Chinese gear and the federal government has banned certain Chinese communications gear, creating a patchwork of restrictions ahead of any coherent national framework.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Procurement risk for Chinese-sourced grid equipment is already jurisdiction-specific, which matters for developers operating multi-state portfolios.

insights.claim: Vault Typhoon is an active, ongoing Chinese campaign with public documented evidence of operators embedded inside US utilities, and they avoid ransomware and malware entirely by living off the land using tools already present on the systems, which makes them extremely hard to detect.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Signature-based and malware-centric detection is structurally blind to this tradecraft, favoring behavioral and network-baseline monitoring vendors in the OT space.
insights.quote: they're not using malware. They're using the tools that already exist. So we call it living off the land.

insights.claim: China's motive for prepositioning is best guessed as leverage to exert influence in a trade or Taiwan scenario, and notably China openly admitted the Salt Typhoon intrusions into nearly every major US telecom backbone without the US treating it as an act of war.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Grid access is a geopolitical bargaining chip that would likely be exercised only alongside a Taiwan or trade escalation, so it is a tail risk correlated with those events.
insights.quote: all we can say is our best guess is ostensibly it is to exert influence over us whether there is a particular trade situation whether there is a particular Taiwan situation

insights.claim: For equipment that cannot be assured, the working practice is to isolate it so it can only talk through a very narrow channel and then monitor everything on that channel, accepting that you cannot prevent everything but can reliably detect.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Detection-over-prevention is the operative doctrine for imported grid gear, which shifts spending toward monitoring and network architecture rather than device replacement.
insights.quote: So you can't prevent it from happening, but you can certainly detect it.

themes.theme: Data centers and all-hazards load risk

insights.claim: NERK issued a level three alert covering what it calls the computational load entity, formally recognizing large data centers as a distinct grid reliability risk category.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: A new regulated entity class for data centers is forming, which will bring interconnection and ride-through obligations to hyperscaler and colocation load.

insights.claim: A data center in PJM recently dropped three gigawatts of load at once and the grid took ten minutes to stabilize, versus the seconds to few minutes typical for most disturbances.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: This is a concrete, unprecedented reliability datapoint that strengthens the case for ride-through mandates and for grid-stabilizing hardware procurement.
insights.quote: recently was the one in PJM a data center dropped three gigawatts

insights.claim: Texas Bitcoin mining farms drew enormous power and then automatically dropped off whenever coin prices hit a threshold, swinging the grid hard, which prompted new rules in that market.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Price-triggered load behavior links crypto markets directly to grid stability, a correlation that regulators are now actively pricing into interconnection rules.

insights.claim: Texas has just passed ride-through standards and NERK is developing a set of its own, and these standards would also defend against an attacker deliberately dropping large loads or generation off the grid.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Ride-through requirements create demand for reserve and stabilization equipment such as static VAR compensators and for compliant inverter firmware.

insights.claim: Grid standards are written from an all-hazards perspective that starts with grid physics and treats cyber as just one hazard alongside squirrels, backhoes, earthquakes and floods, so security controls are justified by physical consequence rather than threat actor identity.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Cyber-specific mandates will keep arriving bundled inside reliability standards, so track NERK reliability rulemaking rather than cyber policy alone.
insights.quote: whether it's a cyber threat whether it's a squirrel whether it's a backhoe you name it

insights.claim: Cyber-informed engineering means reinstalling analog electromechanical relays and protection devices alongside high-precision digital units such as phasor measurement units, accepting lower precision in exchange for a backstop that cannot be hacked.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: A counter-trend toward analog protection hardware is emerging inside an otherwise digitizing grid, which is a niche but real product demand signal.
insights.quote: even if the cyber causes problems physics is still physics

insights.claim: The design principle is to shrink the physical envelope so a malicious command cannot cause harm, illustrated by making a chlorine pipe, pump, battery and reservoir so small that even a command to dump five billion parts per million physically cannot execute.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Consequence-limiting engineering is a reusable mental model for evaluating whether any operator has real resilience or only digital controls.

insights.claim: The analog gates are targeted at protecting equipment that is hardest to replace, including large transformers and big generators that can be desynchronized and resynchronized to torque the shaft, with some models showing an attacker could make a generator explode.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: The tail risk that matters is destruction of long-lead-time equipment, not brief outages, which is what drives utility insurance and replacement exposure.
insights.quote: there's even some that have modeled like actually getting the generator to go boom

insights.claim: There is no rule or requirement to install these analog protections, but most large utilities are doing it as a business decision because replacing a transformer costs hundreds of millions of dollars with a minimum two to three year lead time while Google, Facebook and Amazon are buying equipment ahead of them in the queue.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler equipment buying is lengthening utility replacement queues, turning grid resilience capex into a supply-chain-driven economic imperative rather than a compliance one.
insights.quote: now we're up against, you know, Google and Facebook and Amazon who are buying the equipment out in front of us.

insights.claim: Adoption of these protections is uneven, with some large utilities doing it for their critical equipment and others not, because nothing mandates it.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Resilience quality varies materially between utilities with no disclosure requirement, which is an underpriced differentiator in utility credit and insurance analysis.
insights.quote: there's no rule to do this, no requirement to do this yet

themes.theme: AI risk, incident data and regulatory harmonization

insights.claim: The biggest unanswered concern is that AI has made modeling entire grids computationally cheap, letting an adversary overlay transportation, communications and gas networks and compute the exact sequence of key component attacks needed to trigger a multi-infrastructure cascade.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Cross-infrastructure interdependency is the frontier risk with no current defense, and defenders are only beginning to model the same weaknesses attackers can now compute.
insights.quote: the ability to cause a multi-infrastructure cascade by key component attacks in just the right number and and frequency

insights.claim: CISA's CI Fortify program asks critical infrastructure owners to run exercises on islanding themselves into what the industry calls turtle mode and to determine whether they can keep essential services running for a day or a week without connectivity, but it is a suggestion rather than a requirement.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Islanding capability is becoming the practical resilience benchmark across water, gas, transport and electric, and it is currently voluntary and unevenly adopted.
insights.quote: we in the business we call it turtle mode

insights.claim: Electricity's dependence on gas is deepening because almost all of the new generation being built for AI demand is gas generation, which compounds the multi-infrastructure cascade risk.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: AI-driven gas buildout is creating a single-point interdependency between two critical infrastructures that neither regulator currently governs jointly.
insights.quote: We have a lot of gas generators, especially now for AI. There's almost all of them are going to be gas generators.

insights.claim: Miller laments the budget and staff cuts to CISA because its free templates and information products raise the security floor for the small asset owners who can never hire a security team, and he singles out the known exploited vulnerabilities list as its most valuable output for prioritizing which of a hundred vulnerabilities actually matter.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Shrinking CISA removes the free baseline that small distributed asset owners rely on, widening the gap exactly where the grid is growing fastest.
insights.quote: they can take this template and apply it because it's free from SISA

insights.claim: The single rule change Miller would prioritize is making CIRCIA incident reporting work, because without it there is no actuarial data on what attackers are doing or what defenses actually work, leaving regulators, insurers and operators guessing where to spend.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Absence of actuarial cyber data is why grid cyber insurance and security spend allocation remain unpriced; mandatory reporting would be the unlock.
insights.quote: We don't have any actuarial data without this kind of reporting.

insights.claim: Critical infrastructure cyber regulation is headed in the wrong direction because each infrastructure has its own authoritative body, penalty structure and compliance regime, forcing multi-utility owners into entirely separate compliance organizations and forcing software vendors to write different versions of the same product.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Harmonization would cut duplicated compliance cost across combination utilities and expand the addressable market for a single OT security product line.
insights.quote: Whether it's gas, electric, water, transportation, it's all flow control.

insights.claim: As a former regulator Miller favors regulating only the bare minimum and letting business agreements and insurance underwriting police behavior above that floor, since unreliable partners lose contracts and cannot get insurance for their plants.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Insurance underwriting is an underappreciated de facto grid security regulator, so watch insurer requirements as a faster-moving standard than rulemaking.
insights.quote: I'm a big fan of regulating only absolutely the bare minimum that you have to regulate

insights.claim: Attribution after a US grid event is near certain because utilities are required to keep extensive operational data, insurers send forensics teams to chase the software and hardware liability chain, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission dispatches blackout investigation teams comparable to an NTSB investigation, unlike the Spain blackout where some entities refused to share data or had never logged it.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: Post-event liability will be chased through vendors and software suppliers, not just operators, which puts grid equipment and software makers in the litigation path.
insights.quote: It's like an NTSB investigation.

insights.claim: Miller predicts the current push toward balkanized domestic manufacturing and technology sovereignty will fail and the pendulum will swing back toward open transparency frameworks, using the precedent of encryption export controls being replaced by open, inspectable standards.
insights.speaker: Patrick Miller
insights.so_what: If transparency frameworks win over onshoring mandates, the long-run winners are standards-compliant global suppliers rather than protected domestic champions.
insights.quote: the solution to this is transparency
